# GBLUP models for the real-data analysis

## 1. Objective

This module applies genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP) to the
individual phenotypic BLUPs prepared in R01. Three previously specified
models use different genomic covariance structures, while all models share
the outer assessment partitions established in R03:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{GBLUP-A}:   &\quad y = \mu + a + \varepsilon,\\
\text{GBLUP-AD}:  &\quad y = \mu + a + d + \varepsilon,\\
\text{GBLUP-ADE}: &\quad y = \mu + a + d + aa + \varepsilon.
\end{aligned}
$$

The three prespecified structures are fitted using the same 25 outer
cross-validation splits. For each trait and split, the models use the same
analysis individuals and are evaluated on the same 39 assessment individuals.

The response is the individual BLUP obtained from the preceding phenotypic
mixed-model analysis. Within each genomic fitting task, the 39 assessment BLUPs
are masked before estimating the genomic effects. They are subsequently used
to evaluate held-out predictions. The upstream phenotypic BLUP estimation is
not repeated inside each genomic fold.

The functional workflow is:

**receive aligned genotypes, BLUPs, and validation partitions → construct
genomic relationship matrices → define the three GBLUP structures → organize
the fitting tasks → obtain out-of-fold predictions → examine numerical
diagnostics and predictive metrics → summarize individual rankings → deliver
the results for comparison with the ANN models.**

## 2. Packages and dependencies

The packages below support different stages of the tutorial. `sommer` fits
GBLUP models and constructs genomic relationship matrices; `ggplot2`
produces predictive figures; `ggthemes` provides their graphical theme; and
`kableExtra` adds horizontal scrolling to the wide ranking table. The `knitr`
package, already used to render this document, formats the tables. Input files
and parameter values appear only where they are needed.

```{r packages, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(sommer)   # Fit genomic mixed models.
library(ggplot2)  # Create prediction and diagnostic figures.
library(ggthemes) # Apply a consistent visual theme.
library(kableExtra) # Make wide tables horizontally scrollable.
```

## 3. Genomic data and cross-validation

The analysis receives two saved R objects: a quality-controlled dataset
from R02 and the fixed cross-validation partitions from R03. The first
contains the genotype matrix and the precomputed phenotypic BLUPs; the second
identifies which individuals belong to each analysis and assessment set.
Individual identifiers link genotypes, BLUPs, and predictions throughout the
module.

### 3.1 Input objects

The first `readRDS()` retrieves the processed genotype and phenotype data.
The second retrieves the five-repetition, five-fold outer validation design.
The genotype matrix is then converted to an R matrix, while trait names and
individual identifiers are taken from the previously prepared object; the
pipeline does not reconstruct these inputs.

```{r read-common-data}
common <- readRDS("output/real/audit/preprocessed_real_common.rds")
cv <- readRDS("output/real/validation/real_cv_design.rds")

geno <- as.matrix(common$genotype)
blups <- common$phenotype
traits <- common$traits
ids <- rownames(geno)
```

### 3.2 Outer cross-validation partitions

The assessment assignments are summarized into one row for each outer split.
`Repetition` identifies the repetition, `OuterFold` its fold, and `SplitID`
links that row to the corresponding lists of training and assessment IDs.
Sorting by repetition and fold makes the subsequent task grid easier to read
without modifying the original partitions.

```{r outer-partitions}
# Identify the 25 predefined assessment partitions from R03.
outer_meta <- unique(cv$outer_assignments[, c("Repetition", "OuterFold", "SplitID")])
outer_meta <- outer_meta[order(outer_meta$Repetition, outer_meta$OuterFold), , drop = FALSE]
rownames(outer_meta) <- NULL
```

### 3.3 Input summary

The table summarizes the imported objects. Population size, marker count,
traits, and split count are obtained directly from the data. Training and
assessment sizes are read from the first saved outer split, which follows the
same 156/39 allocation as the other partitions defined in R03. The GBLUP
structures are introduced separately in Section 5.

```{r input-summary}
input_summary <- data.frame(
  Item = c(
    "Individuals",
    "Markers after QC",
    "Traits",
    "Outer splits",
    "Outer analysis size",
    "Outer assessment size"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(geno),
    ncol(geno),
    length(traits),
    nrow(outer_meta),
    length(cv$outer_splits[[1L]]$analysis_ids),
    length(cv$outer_splits[[1L]]$assessment_ids)
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  input_summary,
  format = "html",
  caption = "Common inputs used by the GBLUP models",
  row.names = FALSE,
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

The validation object is consumed without modification. Consequently, A, AD,
and ADE are compared on identical training and held-out individuals.

## 4. Genomic relationship matrices

The genotype matrix received from R02 contains 195 individuals and
20,887 markers retained after quality control. Genomic relationship matrices
transform this individual-by-marker representation into individual-by-individual
relationships.

Each resulting matrix has dimension $195 \times 195$. Its rows and columns
identify the same individuals, and its entries describe genomic relationships
according to the genetic component represented by the matrix.

### 4.1 Genetic components and relationship matrices

| Matrix | Genetic component | Construction |
|:-------|:------------------|:-------------|
| $\mathbf{A}$ | Additive | `sommer::A.mat()` |
| $\mathbf{D}$ | Dominance | `sommer::D.mat()` |
| $\mathbf{E}$ | Additive-by-additive epistasis | `sommer::E.mat(type = "A#A")` |

The additive matrix represents genomic relationships associated with
additive genetic effects. The dominance matrix represents relationships
associated with within-locus dominance effects. The epistatic matrix
represents the additive-by-additive component of interactions between loci.

These matrices define the covariance structures of the corresponding
random genetic effects. They do not directly provide individual genetic
predictions or estimated variance components; those quantities are obtained
when the mixed models are fitted.

### 4.2 Construction of the genomic relationship matrices

The following code constructs the three matrices using the same
quality-controlled marker panel. The argument `min.MAF = 0` does not impose
an additional positive minor allele frequency threshold. The dominance
and epistatic matrices retain the `nishio = TRUE` specification, and
`type = "A#A"` identifies the additive-by-additive epistatic structure.

The matrices are constructed using the genomic information of all 195
individuals. Their construction does not use the phenotypic BLUPs.

The elapsed time is recorded immediately before and after the three
matrix-construction calls. It therefore measures the combined construction
time of A, D, and E.

The individual identifiers are assigned to the rows and columns of each
matrix to maintain correspondence between genomic relationships and the
individuals used in the mixed models.

The code also summarizes matrix dimensions, symmetry, finite entries,
mean diagonal values, and the combined construction time.

Matrix construction is displayed without being repeated during routine
rendering. The numerical summary is retrieved from the previously saved
results.

```{r build-kernels, eval=FALSE}
# Construct additive, dominance, and additive-by-additive kernels.
kernel_start <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
A_matrix <- sommer::A.mat(geno, min.MAF = 0)
D_matrix <- sommer::D.mat(geno, nishio = TRUE, min.MAF = 0)
E_matrix <- sommer::E.mat(geno, nishio = TRUE, type = "A#A", min.MAF = 0)
kernel_seconds <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - kernel_start

# Label rows and columns using the common individual identifiers.
rownames(A_matrix) <- ids
colnames(A_matrix) <- ids
rownames(D_matrix) <- ids
colnames(D_matrix) <- ids
rownames(E_matrix) <- ids
colnames(E_matrix) <- ids

kernel_summary <- data.frame(
  Kernel = c("Additive", "Dominance", "Epistatic_AxA"),
  Rows = c(nrow(A_matrix), nrow(D_matrix), nrow(E_matrix)),
  Columns = c(ncol(A_matrix), ncol(D_matrix), ncol(E_matrix)),
  Symmetric = c(
    isTRUE(all.equal(A_matrix, t(A_matrix), tolerance = 1e-8)),
    isTRUE(all.equal(D_matrix, t(D_matrix), tolerance = 1e-8)),
    isTRUE(all.equal(E_matrix, t(E_matrix), tolerance = 1e-8))
  ),
  Finite = c(all(is.finite(A_matrix)), all(is.finite(D_matrix)),
             all(is.finite(E_matrix))),
  Mean_diagonal = c(mean(diag(A_matrix)), mean(diag(D_matrix)),
                    mean(diag(E_matrix))),
  Kernel_build_seconds = rep(kernel_seconds, 3L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
```

```{r load-kernel-summary, include=FALSE}
kernel_summary <- read.csv("output/real/gblup/real_gblup_kernel_summary.csv",
                           stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

### 4.3 Numerical properties of the relationship matrices

The following table presents the previously saved numerical summaries
of the additive, dominance, and additive-by-additive relationship matrices.

The dimensions describe the number of individuals represented in each
matrix. The symmetry and finite-entry columns provide basic numerical
diagnostics, but these checks alone do not establish positive
semidefiniteness.

```{r show-kernel-summary}
knitr::kable(
  kernel_summary,
  format = "html",
  caption = "Genomic relationship matrices used by the three GBLUP structures",
  digits = 6,
  row.names = FALSE,
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

All three matrices contain 195 rows and 195 columns, are symmetric
within the numerical tolerance used in the code, and contain finite
entries.

The mean diagonal describes the scale of each relationship matrix.
Differences among these values should not be interpreted as differences
in the contribution of additive, dominance, or epistatic effects to
phenotypic variation. The corresponding variance parameters are estimated
during model fitting.

The `Kernel_build_seconds` column contains the same combined construction
time in all three rows. The recorded value of 1.54 seconds corresponds
to the construction of the three matrices together, rather than to
three separately measured execution times.

The following code documents how the numerical summary was saved.

```{r save-kernel-summary, eval=FALSE}
dir.create("output/real/gblup", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(kernel_summary, "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_kernel_summary.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)
```


## 5. Fixed candidate structures

The fitted response is the **precomputed individual phenotypic BLUP**
obtained in R01. The genomic mixed models use the relationship matrices
constructed in Section 4 to specify the covariance of the genetic effects.

### 5.1 Random effects and covariance structures

For the three fixed GBLUP structures, the random effects are described by

$$
\begin{aligned}
a &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_a^2\mathbf{A}),\\
d &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_d^2\mathbf{D}),\\
aa &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{aa}^2\mathbf{E}),\\
\varepsilon &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_e^2\mathbf{I}).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $\mu$ is the intercept, $a$ is the vector of additive genetic
effects, $d$ is the vector of dominance genetic effects, $aa$ is the
vector of additive-by-additive epistatic effects, and $\varepsilon$
is the residual vector.

The matrices $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{D}$, and $\mathbf{E}$ describe
the covariance structure of the corresponding genetic effects, while
$\sigma_a^2$, $\sigma_d^2$, and $\sigma_{aa}^2$ are the associated
variance parameters. The residual covariance is specified by
$\sigma_e^2\mathbf{I}$.

Under the independent random-component specification used in these
models, the marginal covariance matrices of the response are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{V}_{A}
&= \sigma_a^2\mathbf{A}
 + \sigma_e^2\mathbf{I},\\
\mathbf{V}_{AD}
&= \sigma_a^2\mathbf{A}
 + \sigma_d^2\mathbf{D}
 + \sigma_e^2\mathbf{I},\\
\mathbf{V}_{ADE}
&= \sigma_a^2\mathbf{A}
 + \sigma_d^2\mathbf{D}
 + \sigma_{aa}^2\mathbf{E}
 + \sigma_e^2\mathbf{I}.
\end{aligned}
$$

### 5.2 Predictions under each genomic structure

The three models differ in the genetic components included in the
prediction. The predicted response for individual $i$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{y}_{i,A}
&= \widehat{\mu}+\widehat{a}_i,\\
\widehat{y}_{i,AD}
&= \widehat{\mu}+\widehat{a}_i+\widehat{d}_i,\\
\widehat{y}_{i,ADE}
&= \widehat{\mu}+\widehat{a}_i+\widehat{d}_i
+\widehat{aa}_i.
\end{aligned}
$$

The intercept and genetic effects are estimated separately for each
model-fitting task. Their sum provides predictions on the scale of the
individual phenotypic BLUPs. The residual is not included in the
predicted value.

The A model provides the additive reference structure. The AD model
additionally represents dominance relationships, whereas the ADE model
also accommodates additive-by-additive epistatic relationships.

### 5.3 Candidate models used in cross-validation

Each row in the next table identifies a model and the genomic effects
included in its covariance specification. The labels are used unchanged in
the task grid, saved predictions, and later results.

```{r model-structures}
model_structures <- data.frame(
  Structure = c(
    "A",
    "AD",
    "ADE"
  ),
  Model = c(
    "GBLUP_A",
    "GBLUP_AD",
    "GBLUP_ADE"
  ),
  Genomic_components = c(
    "Additive",
    "Additive + dominance",
    "Additive + dominance + additive-by-additive epistasis"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  model_structures,
  format = "html",
  caption = "Fixed GBLUP candidate structures",
  row.names = FALSE,
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

The three structures remain fixed throughout the analysis. Increasing
the number of genetic components provides a more flexible covariance
specification, but does not necessarily improve prediction in held-out
individuals.

Their predictive performance is evaluated using the same validation
partitions, response variables, and predefined metrics.

The next section combines these three genomic structures with the
characteristics and outer cross-validation splits to define the complete
set of model-fitting tasks.

## 6. Evaluation grid

The evaluation grid combines three traits, five repetitions of five outer
folds, and three fixed genomic structures. Each row represents one fitting
task, with 25 tasks per trait-model combination and 75 per trait or model.

$$
3\times5\times5\times3=225\ \text{model-fitting tasks}.
$$

`SplitID` identifies the partition prepared in R03, whereas `TaskID`
identifies the combination of trait, split, and genomic structure.
The code below constructs these combinations and summarizes their counts.

Each task predicts 39 assessment individuals, so the complete design
contains $225\times39=8{,}775$ held-out prediction records. These tasks
are not statistically independent because their analysis sets overlap
across folds and repetitions.

```{r task-grid}
# Cross each characteristic with the 25 splits and three fixed structures.
task_table <- data.frame(
  Dataset = character(0), Trait = character(0), Repetition = integer(0),
  OuterFold = integer(0), SplitID = character(0), Structure = character(0),
  Model = character(0), TaskID = character(0), stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in traits) {
  for (split_row in seq_len(nrow(outer_meta))) {
    for (model_row in seq_len(nrow(model_structures))) {
      split_id <- outer_meta$SplitID[split_row]
      structure <- model_structures$Structure[model_row]
      task_table <- rbind(task_table, data.frame(
        Dataset = "real", Trait = trait,
        Repetition = outer_meta$Repetition[split_row],
        OuterFold = outer_meta$OuterFold[split_row],
        SplitID = split_id, Structure = structure,
        Model = model_structures$Model[model_row],
        TaskID = paste(trait, split_id, structure, sep = "_"),
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      ))
    }
  }
}
rownames(task_table) <- NULL

task_summary <- as.data.frame(table(task_table$Trait, task_table$Structure),
                              stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(task_summary) <- c("Trait", "Structure", "Tasks")

knitr::kable(task_summary, format = "html",
               caption = "Number of outer fitting tasks by trait and GBLUP structure",
               row.names = FALSE,
               table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"')
```

## 7. Fit A, AD, and ADE in every outer split

### 7.1 Analysis and assessment individuals

For each trait and outer split, the partitions received from R03 define
156 analysis individuals and 39 assessment individuals.

| Set | Individuals | Response during genomic fitting |
|:----|------------:|:--------------------------------|
| Analysis | 156 | Available phenotypic BLUPs |
| Assessment | 39 | Masked phenotypic BLUPs |
| Total | 195 | Common genotyped population |

The response vector contains the phenotypic BLUPs estimated in R01.
The data supplied to the genomic model retain all 195 individual
identifiers, but `dat$y[assessment_index] <- NA_real_` masks the 39
assessment responses before fitting. The 156 available BLUPs supply
response information for estimating the model parameters and effects.

The genomic relationship matrices include all 195 genotyped individuals.
Their relationships provide the basis for predicting genetic effects for
individuals with masked responses. The original response vector is retained
separately and its assessment values are recovered only for evaluation.

This is out-of-sample prediction with respect to genomic fitting. The
upstream phenotypic BLUP estimation is not repeated inside each fold.

### 7.2 Model fitting and prediction

The three structures defined in Section 5 are fitted with `sommer::mmes()`.
The formula `y ~ 1` specifies the fixed intercept, and `rcov = ~ units`
specifies the residual structure. The random-effect terms combine `vsm()`
and `ism()` with the genomic covariance matrix supplied through `Gu`.

| Genetic effect | Individual factor | Relationship matrix |
|:---------------|:------------------|:--------------------|
| Additive | `id` | `A_matrix` |
| Dominance | `idd` | `D_matrix` |
| Additive-by-additive | `ide` | `E_matrix` |

The factors identify the same individuals but distinguish the random
genetic components. The numerical settings are identical across tasks.

| Setting | Value | Interpretation |
|:--------|------:|:---------------|
| `SEED_GLOBAL` | 20261105 | Random seed |
| `N_ITERS_SOMMER` | 50 | Maximum number of fitting iterations |
| `TOL_LLIK` | 0.0001 | Tolerance passed to `tolParConvLL` |

After fitting, the code extracts the variance parameters from `fit$theta`
according to the structure. Components absent from a model are stored
as zero; these structural zeros differ from zero estimates of components
that were fitted. The log-likelihood sequence in `fit$llik` and the
convergence indicator in `fit$convergence` provide the numerical
information discussed in Section 8.

The random-effect solutions are recovered from `fit$uList`. The incidence
matrices constructed with `model.matrix()` associate those solutions with
the individual identifiers. For the complete ADE structure,

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{1}\widehat{\mu}
+\mathbf{Z}_a\widehat{\mathbf{a}}
+\mathbf{Z}_d\widehat{\mathbf{d}}
+\mathbf{Z}_{aa}\widehat{\mathbf{aa}}.
$$

The intercept is extracted from `fit$b`. Contributions absent from a model
are represented by zero vectors. The sum of the genetic contributions is
the genomic component; adding the intercept produces predictions on the
phenotypic BLUP scale. The residual is not added to the prediction.

Only the 39 assessment predictions and corresponding observed BLUPs are
used to evaluate each task. The following chunk documents the complete
fitting procedure without rerunning it during routine rendering. The
persisted results are subsequently loaded for the summaries and figures.

```{r fit-all-gblup-models, eval=FALSE}
# Use the same numerical settings for every trait, split, and GBLUP structure.
SEED_GLOBAL <- 20261105L
N_ITERS_SOMMER <- 50L
TOL_LLIK <- 1e-4
set.seed(SEED_GLOBAL)
run_start <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]

result_list <- vector("list", nrow(task_table))
prediction_list <- vector("list", nrow(task_table))

for (i in seq_len(nrow(task_table))) {
  # Locate the outer analysis and assessment individuals.
  task <- task_table[i, , drop = FALSE]
  trait <- task$Trait
  structure <- task$Structure
  split <- cv$outer_splits[[task$SplitID]]
  analysis_index <- match(split$analysis_ids, ids)
  assessment_index <- match(split$assessment_ids, ids)
  response_vector <- blups[[trait]]

  # Mask assessment BLUPs before estimating the genomic effects.
  id_factor <- factor(ids, levels = ids)
  dat <- data.frame(y = response_vector, id = id_factor,
                    idd = id_factor, ide = id_factor)
  dat$y[assessment_index] <- NA_real_

  # Fit one of the three prespecified covariance structures.
  fit_start <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
  if (structure == "A") {
    fit <- sommer::mmes(
      y ~ 1,
      random = ~ vsm(ism(id), Gu = A_matrix),
      rcov = ~ units, nIters = N_ITERS_SOMMER,
      tolParConvLL = TOL_LLIK, data = dat,
      verbose = FALSE, dateWarning = FALSE
    )
  } else if (structure == "AD") {
    fit <- sommer::mmes(
      y ~ 1,
      random = ~ vsm(ism(id), Gu = A_matrix) +
        vsm(ism(idd), Gu = D_matrix),
      rcov = ~ units, nIters = N_ITERS_SOMMER,
      tolParConvLL = TOL_LLIK, data = dat,
      verbose = FALSE, dateWarning = FALSE
    )
  } else {
    fit <- sommer::mmes(
      y ~ 1,
      random = ~ vsm(ism(id), Gu = A_matrix) +
        vsm(ism(idd), Gu = D_matrix) +
        vsm(ism(ide), Gu = E_matrix),
      rcov = ~ units, nIters = N_ITERS_SOMMER,
      tolParConvLL = TOL_LLIK, data = dat,
      verbose = FALSE, dateWarning = FALSE
    )
  }
  fit_seconds <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - fit_start

  # Extract the variance components and numerical diagnostics.
  theta <- as.numeric(fit$theta)
  llik <- as.numeric(fit$llik)
  last_llik_change <- if (length(llik) > 1L) tail(diff(llik), 1L) else NA_real_

  variance_A <- 0
  variance_D <- 0
  variance_E <- 0
  variance_residual <- 0
  if (structure == "A") {
    variance_A <- theta[1L]
    variance_residual <- theta[2L]
  } else if (structure == "AD") {
    variance_A <- theta[1L]
    variance_D <- theta[2L]
    variance_residual <- theta[3L]
  } else {
    variance_A <- theta[1L]
    variance_D <- theta[2L]
    variance_E <- theta[3L]
    variance_residual <- theta[4L]
  }
  any_negative <- any(c(variance_A, variance_D, variance_E, variance_residual) < 0)
  pass_llik_gate <- is.finite(last_llik_change) && abs(last_llik_change) <= TOL_LLIK

  # Recover the individual effects and calculate predictions on the BLUP scale.
  prediction_start <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
  additive <- rep(0, length(ids))
  dominance <- rep(0, length(ids))
  epistatic <- rep(0, length(ids))

  additive_effect <- as.matrix(fit$uList[["vsm(ism(id), Gu = A_matrix)"]])
  additive_incidence <- model.matrix(~ id - 1, data = dat)
  additive <- as.numeric(additive_incidence %*% additive_effect[, 1L, drop = FALSE])

  if (structure %in% c("AD", "ADE")) {
    dominance_effect <- as.matrix(fit$uList[["vsm(ism(idd), Gu = D_matrix)"]])
    dominance_incidence <- model.matrix(~ idd - 1, data = dat)
    dominance <- as.numeric(dominance_incidence %*% dominance_effect[, 1L, drop = FALSE])
  }
  if (structure == "ADE") {
    epistatic_effect <- as.matrix(fit$uList[["vsm(ism(ide), Gu = E_matrix)"]])
    epistatic_incidence <- model.matrix(~ ide - 1, data = dat)
    epistatic <- as.numeric(epistatic_incidence %*% epistatic_effect[, 1L, drop = FALSE])
  }
  genomic_component <- additive + dominance + epistatic
  intercept <- as.numeric(fit$b)[1L]
  predicted_value <- intercept + genomic_component
  predict_seconds <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - prediction_start

  # Evaluate only the 39 individuals withheld from the current fit.
  observed_test <- response_vector[assessment_index]
  predicted_test <- predicted_value[assessment_index]
  constant_prediction <- length(unique(predicted_test)) == 1L

  if (length(unique(observed_test)) > 1L && !constant_prediction) {
    correlation <- cor(predicted_test, observed_test, method = "pearson")
    spearman <- cor(predicted_test, observed_test, method = "spearman")
  } else {
    correlation <- NA_real_
    spearman <- NA_real_
  }
  rmse <- sqrt(mean((predicted_test - observed_test)^2))
  mae <- mean(abs(predicted_test - observed_test))
  bias <- mean(predicted_test - observed_test)
  slope <- if (!constant_prediction) {
    as.numeric(coef(lm(observed_test ~ predicted_test))[2L])
  } else {
    NA_real_
  }

  # Store one row of diagnostics and 39 individual predictions per fit.
  result_list[[i]] <- data.frame(
    Dataset = "real", Trait = trait,
    Repetition = task$Repetition, Fold = task$OuterFold,
    SplitID = task$SplitID, TaskID = task$TaskID,
    Model = task$Model, Structure = structure,
    N_train = length(analysis_index), N_test = length(assessment_index),
    Convergence = isTRUE(fit$convergence), Iterations = length(llik),
    Final_LLik = tail(llik, 1L), Last_LLik_change = last_llik_change,
    Pass_LLik_gate = pass_llik_gate,
    Variance_A = variance_A, Variance_D = variance_D,
    Variance_E = variance_E, Variance_Residual = variance_residual,
    Any_negative = any_negative, Constant_prediction = constant_prediction,
    BLUP_Correlation = correlation, BLUP_Spearman = spearman,
    BLUP_RMSE = rmse, BLUP_MAE = mae, BLUP_Bias = bias, BLUP_Slope = slope,
    Kernel_build_seconds = kernel_seconds, Fit_seconds = fit_seconds,
    Predict_seconds = predict_seconds, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  prediction_list[[i]] <- data.frame(
    Dataset = "real", Trait = trait,
    Repetition = task$Repetition, Fold = task$OuterFold,
    SplitID = task$SplitID, TaskID = task$TaskID,
    Model = task$Model, Structure = structure, ID = ids[assessment_index],
    Observed_BLUP = observed_test, Predicted_BLUP = predicted_test,
    Genomic_Component = genomic_component[assessment_index],
    Additive_Prediction = additive[assessment_index],
    Dominance_Prediction = dominance[assessment_index],
    Epistatic_Prediction = epistatic[assessment_index],
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

}

results <- do.call(rbind, result_list)
predictions <- do.call(rbind, prediction_list)
rownames(results) <- NULL
rownames(predictions) <- NULL
run_seconds <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - run_start
```


```{r load-model-results, include=FALSE}

if (!exists("results", inherits = FALSE)) {
  results <- readRDS("output/real/gblup/real_gblup_results.rds")
  predictions <- readRDS("output/real/gblup/real_gblup_predictions.rds")
  run_metadata <- readRDS("output/real/gblup/real_gblup_run_metadata.rds")
}
```

### 7.3 Model results

Each row of `results` represents one fitting task, identified by trait,
outer split, and genomic structure. The object stores sample sizes,
variance parameters, numerical diagnostics, predictive metrics, and
elapsed times. The first six rows illustrate selected columns of the
225 fitting records.

```{r preview-gblup-results}
knitr::kable(
  head(results[, c("Trait", "SplitID", "Structure", "N_train", "N_test",
                   "BLUP_Correlation", "BLUP_RMSE")]),
  format = "html", digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "First six rows of the GBLUP model results",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

### 7.4 Held-out predictions

Each row of `predictions` represents an assessment individual in a
particular task. `Observed_BLUP` is the held-out response, and
`Predicted_BLUP` includes the intercept and the estimated genetic effects.
`Genomic_Component` excludes the intercept. The additive, dominance,
and epistatic contributions are also stored separately.

There are 39 records per task and 8,775 records in the complete design.
They do not represent 8,775 different individuals because each individual
appears across repetitions, traits, and structures. The first six rows
illustrate the stored predictions.

```{r preview-gblup-predictions}

  caption = "First six held-out GBLUP predictions",
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

### 7.5 Saving the fitting results

The model summaries and individual predictions are saved in CSV and RDS
formats. CSV allows inspection of the numerical records, while RDS retains
the R objects. The run metadata record the software version, numerical
settings, dimensions, and elapsed times. Routine rendering reads persisted
results rather than repeating the 225 adjustments.

The following export code is disabled during routine rendering.



```{r save-gblup-model-results, eval=FALSE}
# Export the 225 model summaries and 8,775 assessment predictions.
dir.create("output/real/gblup", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(results, "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_results.csv", row.names = FALSE)
saveRDS(results, "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_results.rds")
write.csv(predictions, "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_predictions.csv", row.names = FALSE)
saveRDS(predictions, "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_predictions.rds")

# Record the numerical settings, software version, and elapsed run time.
run_metadata <- list(
  dataset = "real", models = c("GBLUP_A", "GBLUP_AD", "GBLUP_ADE"),
  structures = c("A", "AD", "ADE"), seed_global = SEED_GLOBAL,
  sommer_version = as.character(packageVersion("sommer")),
  nIters_sommer = N_ITERS_SOMMER, tolParConvLL = TOL_LLIK,
  marker_panel_n = ncol(geno), individuals_n = nrow(geno),
  traits = traits, outer_splits = nrow(outer_meta),
  tasks = nrow(results), prediction_rows = nrow(predictions),
  kernel_build_seconds = kernel_seconds, total_run_seconds = run_seconds,
  timestamp = as.character(Sys.time())
)
saveRDS(run_metadata, "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_run_metadata.rds")
```

## 8. Numerical behavior

The numerical behavior of each trait-model combination is summarized across
its 25 outer fitting tasks before interpreting predictive performance.

| Diagnostic | Interpretation |
|:-----------|:---------------|
| `Fits` | Number of fitting records |
| `Converged` | Fits with a true `sommer` convergence indicator |
| `Negative_components` | Fits with at least one negative variance estimate |
| `Pass_LLik_gate` | Fits satisfying the additional log-likelihood check |
| `Constant_predictions` | Fits with identical assessment predictions |

The convergence indicator comes from `fit$convergence`. The stored iteration
count is the length of `fit$llik`. When at least two log-likelihood values
are available, the code calculates the final change

$$
\Delta\ell=\ell_t-\ell_{t-1}.
$$

The additional check requires a finite change satisfying
$|\Delta\ell|\leq10^{-4}$. It is distinct from the convergence indicator.
The negative-component diagnostic counts affected fits, not the total
number of negative estimates. These diagnostics describe the original
fits without changing structures or excluding tasks.

```{r numerical-summary}
# Count convergence and other numerical diagnostics by structure and trait.
numerical_summary <- data.frame(
  Structure = character(0), Trait = character(0), Fits = integer(0),
  Converged = integer(0), Negative_components = integer(0),
  Pass_LLik_gate = integer(0), Constant_predictions = integer(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (structure in c("A", "AD", "ADE")) {
  for (trait in traits) {
    x <- results[results$Structure == structure & results$Trait == trait,
                 , drop = FALSE]
    numerical_summary <- rbind(numerical_summary, data.frame(
      Structure = structure, Trait = trait, Fits = nrow(x),
      Converged = sum(x$Convergence),
      Negative_components = sum(x$Any_negative),
      Pass_LLik_gate = sum(x$Pass_LLik_gate),
      Constant_predictions = sum(x$Constant_prediction),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
}

knitr::kable(
  numerical_summary,
  format = "html",
  caption = "Numerical behavior of the fixed GBLUP structures",
  row.names = FALSE,
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

```{r save-numerical-summary, eval=FALSE}
write.csv(numerical_summary,
          "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_numerical_summary.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)
```

In the persisted results, all 225 fits have a true convergence indicator,
while 215 satisfy the additional final log-likelihood-change check.
The ten remaining fits illustrate why these diagnostics must be
interpreted separately.

Five fits contain at least one negative variance estimate, warranting
caution when interpreting their variance parameters. Four fits produce
constant assessment predictions, for which correlations are undefined
but prediction errors can still be evaluated.

These occurrences remain documented in the original results. A true
convergence indicator alone does not establish that every numerical
check was satisfied. The next section examines held-out predictive
performance.

## 9. Held-out predictive performance

### 9.1 Metrics within each outer assessment split

The observed phenotypic BLUPs and their corresponding predictions are
compared within each outer assessment split. Each fitting task provides
39 paired observations. The observed values were masked during genomic
fitting and are used here as the reference response.

| Metric | Interpretation | Reference direction |
|:-------|:---------------|:--------------------|
| Pearson correlation | Linear association between observed and predicted BLUPs | Higher |
| Spearman correlation | Monotonic association based on ranks | Higher |
| RMSE | Quadratic prediction error on the BLUP scale | Lower |
| MAE | Absolute prediction error on the BLUP scale | Lower |
| Bias | Mean signed difference between predicted and observed BLUPs | Close to zero |
| Slope | Calibration slope of observed on predicted BLUPs | Close to one |

Pearson correlation measures association, not equality of the observed
and predicted values. A high correlation may coexist with systematic
bias or differences in scale. Spearman correlation describes the
agreement in ordering within the assessment split.

Let $y_i$ and $\widehat y_i$ be the observed and predicted BLUPs for the
$i$th assessment individual, with $n=39$ in each task. The error metrics
are defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{RMSE}&=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\widehat y_i-y_i)^2},\\
\operatorname{MAE}&=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\widehat y_i-y_i|,\\
\operatorname{Bias}&=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\widehat y_i-y_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

RMSE gives greater weight to large errors than MAE. Positive bias
indicates overprediction on average, whereas negative bias indicates
underprediction. A bias near zero does not imply that individual errors
are small, because positive and negative errors may cancel.

The calibration slope is the estimated coefficient of predicted BLUPs in
an ordinary least-squares regression with an intercept:

$$
y_i=\alpha+\beta\widehat y_i+\epsilon_i.
$$

A slope of one is the reference for calibration of scale, but does not
alone establish calibration of location or individual prediction accuracy.
When a meaningful linear association exists, slopes above one can indicate
insufficient predicted dispersion and slopes below one can indicate
excessive predicted dispersion. Slopes may be unstable when predictions
have little variation.

### 9.2 Aggregation and metric availability

There are 25 outer fitting tasks per trait-model combination. Pearson and
Spearman correlations require variation in both the observed and predicted
values. When predictions are constant, these correlations and the
calibration slope are undefined and stored as `NA`. RMSE, MAE, and bias
remain computable for the finite observed and predicted values.

The summary counts finite values with `is.finite()` and uses
`mean(..., na.rm = TRUE)` and, for Pearson and Spearman, `sd(..., na.rm = TRUE)`.
In the saved results, undefined metrics are missing and there are no
infinite metric values. Thus the finite-value counts correspond to the
numbers of observations contributing to the reported means.

For a metric $M$, let $\mathcal{S}_M$ be the splits with a defined value and
$K_M=|\mathcal{S}_M|$. Its mean in these results is

$$
\overline{M}=\frac{1}{K_M}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}_M}M_k.
$$

This is a mean of split-level metrics, not a metric calculated after pooling
all predictions. In particular, the mean split RMSE is generally different
from the RMSE of pooled prediction errors.

The reported standard deviations for Pearson and Spearman describe
variation across the contributing splits, not standard errors or confidence
intervals. The repeated cross-validation tasks are dependent because the
analysis sets overlap.

The following code summarizes the stored metrics for each trait and model.
The denominator columns identify how many splits contribute to each metric.

```{r performance-summary}
# Summarize each metric across its finite outer-split observations.
performance_summary <- data.frame(
  Structure = character(0), Model = character(0), Trait = character(0),
  Splits = integer(0), Correlation_N = integer(0),
  BLUP_Correlation = numeric(0), BLUP_Correlation_SD = numeric(0),
  Spearman_N = integer(0), BLUP_Spearman = numeric(0),
  BLUP_Spearman_SD = numeric(0), RMSE_N = integer(0),
  BLUP_RMSE = numeric(0), MAE_N = integer(0), BLUP_MAE = numeric(0),
  Bias_N = integer(0), BLUP_Bias = numeric(0),
  Slope_N = integer(0), BLUP_Slope = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (structure in c("A", "AD", "ADE")) {
  for (trait in traits) {
    x <- results[results$Structure == structure & results$Trait == trait,
                 , drop = FALSE]
    model_name <- unique(x$Model)
    performance_summary <- rbind(performance_summary, data.frame(
      Structure = structure, Model = model_name, Trait = trait,
      Splits = nrow(x),
      Correlation_N = sum(is.finite(x$BLUP_Correlation)),
      BLUP_Correlation = mean(x$BLUP_Correlation, na.rm = TRUE),
      BLUP_Correlation_SD = sd(x$BLUP_Correlation, na.rm = TRUE),
      Spearman_N = sum(is.finite(x$BLUP_Spearman)),
      BLUP_Spearman = mean(x$BLUP_Spearman, na.rm = TRUE),
      BLUP_Spearman_SD = sd(x$BLUP_Spearman, na.rm = TRUE),
      RMSE_N = sum(is.finite(x$BLUP_RMSE)),
      BLUP_RMSE = mean(x$BLUP_RMSE, na.rm = TRUE),
      MAE_N = sum(is.finite(x$BLUP_MAE)),
      BLUP_MAE = mean(x$BLUP_MAE, na.rm = TRUE),
      Bias_N = sum(is.finite(x$BLUP_Bias)),
      BLUP_Bias = mean(x$BLUP_Bias, na.rm = TRUE),
      Slope_N = sum(is.finite(x$BLUP_Slope)),
      BLUP_Slope = mean(x$BLUP_Slope, na.rm = TRUE),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
}

knitr::kable(
  performance_summary,
  format = "html",
  caption = "Mean held-out performance of A, AD, and ADE across the 25 outer splits",
  digits = 4,
  row.names = FALSE
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    full_width = TRUE,
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "bordered")
  ) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

```{r save-performance-summary, eval=FALSE}
write.csv(performance_summary,
          "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_performance_summary.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)
```

### 9.3 Interpretation of predictive performance

For Cer and BM, all six metrics are available in all 25 splits for each
model. For LP, Pearson, Spearman and slope are available in 23 splits for
A and 24 splits each for AD and ADE. The four remaining tasks have constant
predictions. RMSE, MAE and bias remain available for all 25 splits in every
trait-model combination. None of the 225 fitting tasks is discarded.

The A structure has the largest mean Pearson correlation for all three
traits in the saved results. The differences for Cer are particularly
small. This pattern does not imply that A is best for every metric: AD,
for example, has a slightly smaller mean MAE for BM.

The structures share the same planned outer partitions, but the sets of
splits contributing to a metric may differ when that metric is undefined.
In particular, differences between the reported LP correlation means are
not necessarily contrasts calculated on identical subsets of splits.
No statistical significance or model superiority is established by these
descriptive summaries. Comparisons of error magnitudes also need to respect
the different scales of the traits.

The final comparison module examines the GBLUP and regularized ANN results
on the common validation design. The next section changes the unit of
analysis from outer fitting tasks to individual rankings.

## 10. Out-of-fold ranking of the 195 individuals

### 10.1 Individual out-of-fold predictions

Within each repetition, every individual appears in exactly one outer
assessment fold. Across the five repetitions, this produces five
out-of-fold (OOF) predictions per individual, trait, and genomic structure.
The observed phenotypic BLUP is the same reference value across those
repetitions.

For individual $i$, let $\widehat y_{ir}$ denote the held-out prediction
in repetition $r$. The individual prediction used in the ranking is

$$
\overline{\widehat y}_i=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{r=1}^{5}\widehat y_{ir}.
$$

The object also retains `Prediction_SD`, the sample standard deviation of
the five predictions, and `N_OOF`, the number of contributing predictions.
This standard deviation describes variation across the repeated genomic
fits; it is not a standard error or a prediction interval.

| Unit | Records |
|:-----|--------:|
| OOF predictions per individual, trait and model | 5 |
| Individual ranking records per trait and model | 195 |
| Trait-model combinations | 9 |
| Individual ranking records across all combinations | 1,755 |
| Original held-out prediction records | 8,775 |

Each of the 1,755 records in the saved individual ranking has `N_OOF = 5`.
The ranking uses the mean of the five predicted BLUPs, including the
estimated intercept of each fit. It does not average fold-specific ranks
or use only the genomic component. The five predictions were obtained
while the corresponding individual was outside the genomic fitting sample.

### 10.2 Ranking and upper-20% agreement

The observed and predicted BLUPs are ranked separately in decreasing order
within each trait-model combination. Rank 1 corresponds to the largest
value, and tied values receive their average rank through
`ties.method = "average"`.

Let $R_i$ be the observed rank and $\widehat R_i$ the predicted rank.
The rank difference and absolute rank error are

$$
D_i=\widehat R_i-R_i,\qquad E_i=|D_i|.
$$

A positive difference places the individual farther down the descending
predicted ranking than in the observed ranking. The mean and median of
$E_i$ describe displacement in rank positions across the 195 individuals.

The global ranking Spearman correlation is calculated across the 195
observed and predicted ranks. It differs from the mean split-level
Spearman correlation in Section 9, which summarizes correlations calculated
separately within the 39 assessment individuals of each split.

Upper-20% agreement compares the sets of 39 individuals with the largest
observed and predicted BLUPs. Let $S_o$ and $S_p$ denote those two sets.

$$
\operatorname{Overlap}_N=|S_o\cap S_p|,\qquad
\operatorname{Overlap}_{\mathrm{rate}}=\frac{|S_o\cap S_p|}{39}.
$$

The rate is the fraction of the observed upper group recovered by the
predicted upper group, not a correlation or a chance-corrected index.
The individual ID is used as a deterministic secondary ordering criterion
when selecting the upper group, so both sets contain exactly 39 individuals
regardless of ties. This tie-breaking rule does not change the average
ranks used for rank errors and global Spearman correlation.

The descending order is the same for all traits in the implemented analysis.
The upper group therefore means the largest BLUPs, not necessarily the most
biologically desirable individuals. In a breeding objective favoring lower
trait values, the desirable group would instead be at the lower end. The
present analysis measures agreement under the original descending rule;
it does not reverse trait directions or redefine the saved groups.

The following code constructs the individual ranking and its summary using
the persisted held-out predictions.

```{r individual-ranking}
# Each individual has five OOF predictions for every model and trait.
TOP20_N <- 39L
individual_ranking <- data.frame(
  Structure = character(0), Model = character(0), Trait = character(0),
  ID = character(0), Observed_BLUP = numeric(0),
  Predicted_BLUP = numeric(0), Prediction_SD = numeric(0),
  N_OOF = integer(0), Observed_Rank = numeric(0),
  Predicted_Rank = numeric(0), Rank_Difference = numeric(0),
  Absolute_Rank_Error = numeric(0), Observed_Top20 = logical(0),
  Predicted_Top20 = logical(0), stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
ranking_summary <- data.frame(
  Structure = character(0), Model = character(0), Trait = character(0),
  Individuals = integer(0), Ranking_Spearman = numeric(0),
  Mean_Absolute_Rank_Error = numeric(0),
  Median_Absolute_Rank_Error = numeric(0), Top20_N = integer(0),
  Top20_Overlap_N = integer(0), Top20_Overlap_Rate = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (structure in c("A", "AD", "ADE")) {
  for (trait in traits) {
    x <- predictions[predictions$Structure == structure &
                     predictions$Trait == trait, , drop = FALSE]
    model_name <- unique(x$Model)
    ranking_group <- data.frame(
      Structure = character(0), Model = character(0), Trait = character(0),
      ID = character(0), Observed_BLUP = numeric(0),
      Predicted_BLUP = numeric(0), Prediction_SD = numeric(0),
      N_OOF = integer(0), stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )

    # Average the five assessment predictions for each individual.
    for (individual_id in ids) {
      xi <- x[x$ID == individual_id, , drop = FALSE]
      ranking_group <- rbind(ranking_group, data.frame(
        Structure = structure, Model = model_name, Trait = trait,
        ID = individual_id, Observed_BLUP = unique(xi$Observed_BLUP),
        Predicted_BLUP = mean(xi$Predicted_BLUP),
        Prediction_SD = sd(xi$Predicted_BLUP), N_OOF = nrow(xi),
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      ))
    }

    # Compare descending rankings and the selected upper 20% of individuals.
    ranking_group$Observed_Rank <- rank(-ranking_group$Observed_BLUP,
                                        ties.method = "average")
    ranking_group$Predicted_Rank <- rank(-ranking_group$Predicted_BLUP,
                                         ties.method = "average")
    ranking_group$Rank_Difference <- ranking_group$Predicted_Rank -
      ranking_group$Observed_Rank
    ranking_group$Absolute_Rank_Error <- abs(ranking_group$Rank_Difference)

    observed_order <- order(-ranking_group$Observed_BLUP, ranking_group$ID)
    predicted_order <- order(-ranking_group$Predicted_BLUP, ranking_group$ID)
    ranking_group$Observed_Top20 <- FALSE
    ranking_group$Predicted_Top20 <- FALSE
    ranking_group$Observed_Top20[observed_order[seq_len(TOP20_N)]] <- TRUE
    ranking_group$Predicted_Top20[predicted_order[seq_len(TOP20_N)]] <- TRUE

    top20_overlap_n <- sum(ranking_group$Observed_Top20 &
                           ranking_group$Predicted_Top20)
    top20_overlap_rate <- top20_overlap_n / TOP20_N
    individual_ranking <- rbind(individual_ranking, ranking_group)
    ranking_summary <- rbind(ranking_summary, data.frame(
      Structure = structure, Model = model_name, Trait = trait,
      Individuals = nrow(ranking_group),
      Ranking_Spearman = cor(ranking_group$Observed_Rank,
                             ranking_group$Predicted_Rank, method = "spearman"),
      Mean_Absolute_Rank_Error = mean(ranking_group$Absolute_Rank_Error),
      Median_Absolute_Rank_Error = median(ranking_group$Absolute_Rank_Error),
      Top20_N = TOP20_N, Top20_Overlap_N = top20_overlap_n,
      Top20_Overlap_Rate = top20_overlap_rate,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
}
rownames(individual_ranking) <- NULL
rownames(ranking_summary) <- NULL

knitr::kable(
  ranking_summary,
  format = "html",
  caption = "Agreement between observed and out-of-fold predicted rankings of the 195 individuals",
  digits = 4,
  row.names = FALSE
) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(full_width = TRUE,
                            bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")
```

```{r save-individual-ranking, eval=FALSE}
write.csv(individual_ranking,
          "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_individual_ranking.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)
saveRDS(individual_ranking,
        "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_individual_ranking.rds")
write.csv(ranking_summary,
          "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_ranking_summary.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)
```

### 10.3 Interpretation of the ranking summary

For Cer, the three models recover 22 of the 39 individuals in the observed
upper group (56.41%). For BM, A, AD and ADE recover 11, 10 and 9 individuals,
respectively. For LP, they recover 5, 4 and 4 individuals, respectively.

These overlap counts measure agreement at a fixed selection intensity.
They do not establish agreement over the entire population. Global Spearman
correlation and the mean and median absolute rank errors provide complementary
information. For BM, for example, AD has a slightly higher global Spearman
correlation than A, whereas A recovers more individuals in the observed upper
group. The criteria should therefore be interpreted separately.

The comparisons are descriptive and do not establish statistical differences
among genomic structures or expected selection gains. The wide summary table
can be inspected by horizontal scrolling. Section 11 presents the distributions
of split-level performance and the individual out-of-fold predictions.

## 11. Predictive distributions across outer splits

The following figures summarize predictive performance across the outer
assessment splits for Cer, BM, and LP. The data come from the stored fitting
results described in Sections 7 to 9, without repeating model fitting.

In the boxplots, each point represents one outer fitting task for the
corresponding trait and genomic structure. The box summarizes the median
and interquartile range, and the whiskers follow the usual 1.5-IQR rule.
The points are displaced horizontally for readability using a fixed jitter
seed; the metric values on the vertical axis are unchanged.

The individual-level scatterplot at the end of this section uses the mean
of the five out-of-fold predictions described in Section 10.

### 11.1 Pearson correlation

Pearson correlation measures linear association between observed and predicted
BLUPs within each assessment split. The following code retains only finite
correlations and orders the models as A, AD, and ADE. All trait panels use
the theoretical correlation scale from -1 to 1. The dashed horizontal line
marks zero linear correlation.

```{r performance-figures}
# Generate figure objects from persisted predictions and split metrics.
plot_results <- results

plot_results$Structure <- factor(plot_results$Structure, levels = c("A", "AD", "ADE"))

plot_results$Trait <- factor(plot_results$Trait, levels = traits)

correlation_plot <- ggplot(
  plot_results[is.finite(plot_results$BLUP_Correlation), , drop = FALSE],
  aes(
    x = Structure,
    y = BLUP_Correlation
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    outlier.shape = NA
  ) +
  geom_jitter(
    position = position_jitter(
      width = 0.12,
      height = 0,
      seed = 20261105L
    ),
    size = 1.6,
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ Trait,
    scales = "fixed",
    nrow = 1
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(-1, 1),
    breaks = seq(-1, 1, by = 0.5)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "GBLUP structure",
    y = "Pearson correlation",
    title = "Held-out Pearson correlation across outer splits"
  ) +
  ggthemes::theme_gdocs() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

```{r show-correlation-figure, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="Pearson correlation between observed BLUPs and held-out GBLUP predictions across outer splits, by trait and genomic structure. All panels use the same correlation scale; the dashed line marks zero.", fig.alt="Three faceted boxplots with individual split points showing held-out Pearson correlations for A, AD, and ADE, separately for Cer, BM, and LP, on a common scale from minus one to one with a dashed zero line."}
print(correlation_plot)
```

The 221 defined correlations comprise 75 points for Cer, 75 for BM,
and 71 for LP. The four undefined LP correlations are not plotted.
The common vertical scale makes differences in correlation among traits
visible, while each boxplot summarizes the contributing splits.

The following chunk documents the TIFF export settings without overwriting
the saved figure during routine rendering.

```{r save-correlation-figure, eval=FALSE}
dir.create("output/real/gblup/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "output/real/gblup/figures/real_gblup_correlation_by_model_trait.tiff",
  plot = correlation_plot,
  width = 9,
  height = 5.5,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300,
  compression = "lzw"
)
```

### 11.2 Spearman correlation

Spearman correlation measures monotonic association based on ranks within
each assessment split. The figure retains the finite values and uses the
same vertical scale and zero reference as the Pearson figure, so both
correlation distributions can be inspected on a comparable scale.

```{r build-spearman-figure}
spearman_plot <- ggplot(
  plot_results[is.finite(plot_results$BLUP_Spearman), , drop = FALSE],
  aes(
    x = Structure,
    y = BLUP_Spearman
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    outlier.shape = NA
  ) +
  geom_jitter(
    position = position_jitter(
      width = 0.12,
      height = 0,
      seed = 20261105L
    ),
    size = 1.6,
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ Trait,
    scales = "fixed",
    nrow = 1
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(-1, 1),
    breaks = seq(-1, 1, by = 0.5)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "GBLUP structure",
    y = "Spearman correlation",
    title = "Held-out Spearman correlation across outer splits"
  ) +
  ggthemes::theme_gdocs() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

```{r show-spearman-figure, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="Spearman rank correlation between observed BLUPs and held-out GBLUP predictions across outer splits, by trait and genomic structure. All panels use the same correlation scale; the dashed line marks zero.", fig.alt="Three faceted boxplots with individual split points showing held-out Spearman correlations for A, AD, and ADE, separately for Cer, BM, and LP, on a common scale from minus one to one with a dashed zero line."}
print(spearman_plot)
```

As with Pearson correlation, the figure contains 221 defined values.
The four constant-prediction tasks for LP have undefined Spearman
correlations and are not represented by points. These distributions describe
variation across splits, rather than the global individual ranking in
Section 10.

The export code preserves the original TIFF filename, dimensions,
resolution, and compression.

```{r save-spearman-figure, eval=FALSE}
dir.create("output/real/gblup/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "output/real/gblup/figures/real_gblup_spearman_by_model_trait.tiff",
  plot = spearman_plot,
  width = 9,
  height = 5.5,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300,
  compression = "lzw"
)
```

### 11.3 Root mean squared error

RMSE measures prediction error on the BLUP scale. Unlike correlation, its
magnitude depends on the scale of the trait. Each panel therefore retains
its own vertical scale, shared by the three genomic structures within that
trait. Comparisons of RMSE magnitude should be made within a trait.

```{r build-rmse-figure}
rmse_plot <- ggplot(
  plot_results,
  aes(
    x = Structure,
    y = BLUP_RMSE
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    outlier.shape = NA
  ) +
  geom_jitter(
    position = position_jitter(
      width = 0.12,
      height = 0,
      seed = 20261105L
    ),
    size = 1.6,
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ Trait,
    scales = "free_y",
    nrow = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "GBLUP structure",
    y = "RMSE (BLUP scale)",
    title = "Held-out RMSE across outer splits"
  ) +
  ggthemes::theme_gdocs() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

```{r show-rmse-figure, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="Root mean squared error of held-out GBLUP predictions across outer splits, by trait and genomic structure. Vertical scales are specific to each trait.", fig.alt="Three faceted boxplots with individual split points showing held-out RMSE for A, AD, and ADE, separately for Cer, BM, and LP, with trait-specific vertical scales."}
print(rmse_plot)
```

All 225 fitting tasks contribute to this figure, including the four LP
tasks with constant predictions. The panels describe error variation across
the assessment splits without implying statistical differences among models.

The following export code retains the original TIFF settings.

```{r save-rmse-figure, eval=FALSE}
dir.create("output/real/gblup/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "output/real/gblup/figures/real_gblup_rmse_by_model_trait.tiff",
  plot = rmse_plot,
  width = 9,
  height = 5.5,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300,
  compression = "lzw"
)
```

### 11.4 Observed versus predicted BLUPs

The following figure compares the individual phenotypic BLUPs with the mean
of the five out-of-fold predictions described in Section 10. Each point
represents one individual, with 195 points per trait-model panel and 1,755
points across the nine panels.

The observed BLUP is displayed on the horizontal axis and the mean
out-of-fold predicted BLUP on the vertical axis. Traits occupy the rows
(Cer, BM, and LP), and genomic structures occupy the columns (A, AD, and ADE).

For each trait, the minimum and maximum of the observed and predicted BLUPs
across all three structures define a common plotting range. Two invisible
reference points at these endpoints are supplied to `geom_blank()` for each
panel. They train the scales but do not appear in the scatterplot or enter
any statistical calculation. Both axes receive the same 5% expansion at
both ends, and each panel is square.

Consequently, the three models for a trait share the same horizontal and
vertical limits, while different traits retain their own ranges. The dashed
identity line represents equality between observed and predicted values.
The original individual ranking is not modified, and no BLUP is rescaled
or excluded.

```{r build-observed-predicted-figure}
# Prepare a plotting copy, preserving the original individual ranking.
observed_predicted_data <- individual_ranking
observed_predicted_data$Trait <- factor(
  observed_predicted_data$Trait,
  levels = c("Cer", "BM", "LP")
)
observed_predicted_data$Structure <- factor(
  observed_predicted_data$Structure,
  levels = c("A", "AD", "ADE")
)

# Compute a common range of observed and predicted BLUPs for each trait.
# Repeat the two endpoints for each of the three model panels.
observed_predicted_bounds <- data.frame(
  Trait = character(0),
  Structure = character(0),
  Observed_BLUP = numeric(0),
  Predicted_BLUP = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (trait in levels(observed_predicted_data$Trait)) {
  trait_data <- observed_predicted_data[
    observed_predicted_data$Trait == trait, , drop = FALSE
  ]
  trait_range <- range(c(trait_data$Observed_BLUP,
                         trait_data$Predicted_BLUP))

  observed_predicted_bounds <- rbind(
    observed_predicted_bounds,
    data.frame(
      Trait = rep(trait, 6),
      Structure = rep(c("A", "AD", "ADE"), each = 2),
      Observed_BLUP = rep(trait_range, 3),
      Predicted_BLUP = rep(trait_range, 3),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  )
}

observed_predicted_bounds$Trait <- factor(
  observed_predicted_bounds$Trait,
  levels = levels(observed_predicted_data$Trait)
)
observed_predicted_bounds$Structure <- factor(
  observed_predicted_bounds$Structure,
  levels = levels(observed_predicted_data$Structure)
)

observed_predicted_plot <- ggplot(
  observed_predicted_data,
  aes(
    x = Observed_BLUP,
    y = Predicted_BLUP
  )
) +
  geom_blank(data = observed_predicted_bounds) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    size = 1.5,
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    vars(Trait, Structure),
    ncol = 3,
    scales = "free"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.05)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.05)) +
  labs(
    x = "Observed individual BLUP",
    y = "Mean out-of-fold predicted BLUP",
    title = "Observed and predicted individual BLUPs"
  ) +
  ggthemes::theme_gdocs() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    aspect.ratio = 1
  )
```

```{r show-observed-predicted-figure, fig.width=12, fig.height=11, fig.cap="Observed individual BLUPs versus mean out-of-fold predicted BLUPs for all 195 individuals, by trait and GBLUP structure. Within each trait, all three model panels use identical horizontal and vertical scales. The dashed line indicates equality.", fig.alt="Nine scatterplot panels arranged by Cer, BM, and LP and by A, AD, and ADE, comparing observed BLUPs with mean out-of-fold predicted BLUPs and showing a dashed identity line in square panels with common axis limits within each trait."}
print(observed_predicted_plot)
```

Points above the identity line have predicted BLUPs greater than their
observed BLUPs, whereas points below it have smaller predicted values.
The predicted values are less dispersed than the observed values in the
persisted results, especially for BM and LP. The common scales within each
trait make this difference visible without independently stretching the
prediction axis. These panels describe individual OOF predictions and
complement the split-level correlations and error metrics in Section 9
and the ranking summaries in Section 10.

The following chunk documents the TIFF export with dimensions of 12 by
11 inches, 300 dpi, and LZW compression. It remains disabled during routine
rendering.

```{r save-observed-predicted-figure, eval=FALSE}
dir.create("output/real/gblup/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  filename = "output/real/gblup/figures/real_gblup_observed_vs_predicted_by_model_trait.tiff",
  plot = observed_predicted_plot,
  width = 12,
  height = 11,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300,
  compression = "lzw"
)
```

## 12. Prediction results and saved outputs

### 12.1 Synthesis of the GBLUP results

The three GBLUP structures were evaluated using the same 195 individuals,
three traits, and 25 outer partitions. The 225 fitting tasks and 8,775
held-out predictions provide a common reference for comparing additive,
dominance, and additive-by-additive genomic structures. The five predictions
for each individual, trait, and structure yield 1,755 individual ranking
records.

The results in Sections 8 to 11 support the following descriptive conclusions:

- Mean Pearson correlation is highest for A in each trait, with particularly
  small differences among the three structures for Cer. The inclusion of
  additional genetic components does not consistently improve the evaluated
  predictive metrics.
- Cer has the highest mean correlations and global ranking agreement among
  the three traits. All structures recover 22 of the 39 individuals in its
  observed upper group. The agreement is lower for BM and LP.
- For BM, AD has a slightly lower mean MAE and a higher global ranking
  Spearman correlation than A, whereas A recovers more individuals in the
  observed upper group. Different metrics therefore describe different
  aspects of predictive performance.
- All 225 fits report convergence, but only 215 satisfy the additional
  final log-likelihood-change check. Five fits contain negative estimated
  variance components and four have constant predictions. These diagnostics
  remain documented without deleting fitting records.

The results describe prediction of precomputed individual phenotypic BLUPs
within the represented population. Phenotypic BLUP estimation was not
repeated within each genomic assessment fold. The overlapping training sets
make repeated cross-validation tasks dependent. For LP, correlations and
calibration slopes are undefined in some splits, so means for different
structures may summarize different subsets of the common planned partitions.
The comparisons do not establish statistical superiority, external-population
performance, or expected genetic gain. The descending rankings identify large
BLUPs, not necessarily the biologically desirable direction for each trait.

### 12.2 Numerical outputs and their downstream use

The table generated below identifies the eight principal saved objects.
The result table contains 225 fitting records; the prediction table contains
8,775 held-out records; and the individual ranking contains 1,755 records.
The kernel summary contains three rows, and the numerical, performance, and
ranking summaries each contain nine rows. Run metadata are stored as an R
object rather than as a table of fitting records.

The table caption refers to the downstream comparison. Specifically, R05
reads the three RDS files for results, predictions, and individual rankings;
the other files support interpretation and reproducibility of R04A.

```{r output-inventory}
output_inventory <- data.frame(
  Object = c(
    "Results",
    "Predictions",
    "Individual ranking",
    "Kernel summary",
    "Numerical summary",
    "Performance summary",
    "Ranking summary",
    "Run metadata"
  ),
  Expected_rows = c(
    nrow(results),
    nrow(predictions),
    nrow(individual_ranking),
    nrow(kernel_summary),
    nrow(numerical_summary),
    nrow(performance_summary),
    nrow(ranking_summary),
    NA_integer_
  ),
  Path = c(
    "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_results.rds",
    "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_predictions.rds",
    "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_individual_ranking.rds",
    "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_kernel_summary.csv",
    "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_numerical_summary.csv",
    "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_performance_summary.csv",
    "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_ranking_summary.csv",
    "output/real/gblup/real_gblup_run_metadata.rds"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  output_inventory,
  format = "html",
  caption = "Outputs passed to the downstream real-data comparison",
  row.names = FALSE,
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="width:100%;"'
)
```

The complete numerical inventory is listed below. Paths are relative to
`output/real/gblup/`.

| File(s) | Purpose |
|:--------|:--------|
| `real_gblup_results.rds`, `real_gblup_results.csv` | Split-level results and diagnostics; RDS read by R05 |
| `real_gblup_predictions.rds`, `real_gblup_predictions.csv` | Held-out BLUP predictions and genetic contributions; RDS read by R05 |
| `real_gblup_individual_ranking.rds`, `real_gblup_individual_ranking.csv` | Individual OOF predictions and rankings; RDS read by R05 |
| `real_gblup_kernel_summary.csv` | Numerical properties of A, D, and E |
| `real_gblup_numerical_summary.csv` | Model-fitting diagnostics |
| `real_gblup_performance_summary.csv` | Split-level predictive metric summaries |
| `real_gblup_ranking_summary.csv` | Global ranking agreement and upper-group overlap |
| `real_gblup_run_metadata.rds` | Fitting settings, software and execution metadata |

CSV files allow inspection of the numerical records, while RDS files retain
R objects. The fitting and numerical export chunks are disabled during routine
rendering; the tutorial uses the persisted fitting results and predictions to
construct its summaries and figures.

### 12.3 Figure outputs

The four figure exports described in Section 11 use TIFF format, 300 dpi,
and LZW compression. Paths below are relative to `output/real/gblup/figures/`.
The dimensions refer to the export settings in the current code.

| Figure file | Width x height (inches) | Pixels at 300 dpi |
|:------------|:------------------------|:------------------|
| `real_gblup_correlation_by_model_trait.tiff` | 9 x 5.5 | 2700 x 1650 |
| `real_gblup_spearman_by_model_trait.tiff` | 9 x 5.5 | 2700 x 1650 |
| `real_gblup_rmse_by_model_trait.tiff` | 9 x 5.5 | 2700 x 1650 |
| `real_gblup_observed_vs_predicted_by_model_trait.tiff` | 12 x 11 | 3600 x 3300 |

The export chunks use `eval=FALSE`. Routine rendering displays the current
plot objects without overwriting the saved TIFF files. To update the TIFFs,
execute the corresponding export chunks explicitly after constructing and
checking the current plots. Existing TIFFs reflect the last explicit export,
not necessarily the latest graphical settings in the source.

### 12.4 Continuity of the real-data analysis

[R01 - Phenotypes](real_data_phenotype.html) estimates the individual
phenotypic BLUPs. [R02 - Data preprocessing](real_data_audit.html) prepares
the common marker and phenotype data, and
[R03 - Pre-validation](real_data_validation.html) defines the fixed outer
and inner partitions. R04A uses those common inputs to fit A, AD, and ADE
in the outer analysis sets and assess their predictions in the corresponding
assessment sets.

[R04B - Regularized ANN](real_data_ann.html) reads the same R02 and R03
inputs independently of the GBLUP output files. The ANN analysis uses the
inner folds for model selection within each outer analysis set and the outer
assessment sets for evaluation.

[R05 - Model comparison](real_data_comparison.html) reads the three GBLUP
RDS objects identified above together with the corresponding ANN objects.
It uses the common split and individual identifiers to compare the two model
families, preserving the distinction between split-level metrics and
individual OOF rankings.
